$comment: Branching stories (kind 'story'). Each node: text, speaker, mood, choices [{text, next, points, feedback}]. A node with no choices ends the story. Score = points earned / maxPoints.

a.speaker: Max
a.text: Hi! My bike is broken and I need to get to soccer. Can I borrow yours today? I'll bring it back by dinner.

choices.text: Sure! Please bring it back by dinner.
choices.feedback: Lending to a friend with a clear plan is kind and fair.

choices.text: Only if you pay me $50 for the afternoon.
choices.feedback: That's way too much for one afternoon! Fair deals matter.

b.speaker: Narwhal
b.text: Max brought your bike back right on time, clean and safe! Next week Max asks to borrow it again.

choices.text: Yes! Max kept the promise last time.
choices.feedback: Exactly! When people pay back on time, we trust them more. Banks work the same way with credit.

choices.text: No, I don’t want to lend it ever again.
choices.feedback: That's okay, but Max proved they're trustworthy. Trust grows when promises are kept.

b2.speaker: Max
b2.text: Fifty dollars?! That's more than a new tire costs. I'll ask someone else…

choices.text: Okay, okay, you can borrow it for free if you bring it back by dinner.
choices.feedback: Being fair helps everyone.

c.speaker: Narwhal
c.text: Here's the big idea: when grown-ups borrow from a bank and pay back ON TIME, the bank trusts them more and lends at a lower cost. That trust is called CREDIT. Which friend would a bank trust more?

choices.text: A friend who always pays back on time
choices.feedback: Yes! Paying back on time builds good credit.

choices.text: A friend who forgets to pay back
choices.feedback: Forgetting to pay back hurts trust (and credit). On-time is the key!

end.speaker: Narwhal
end.text: Great thinking! Borrowing is a promise. Keep your promises and people (and banks) will trust you.

a.speaker: Narwhal
a.text: You made $30 at your lemonade stand! What do you do first?

choices.text: Put some in my Save jar
choices.feedback: Paying yourself first is a great habit!

choices.text: Spend it all on candy
choices.feedback: Candy is fun, but then nothing is left for later.

b.speaker: Narwhal
b.text: Your lemons cost $10. How much profit did you really make?

choices.feedback: Right! $30 − $10 = $20 profit.
Remember to subtract what you spent on lemons: $30 − $10 = $20.

c.speaker: Narwhal
c.text: A friend says: give me your $20 and I'll give you $100 next week! What do you do?

choices.text: No thanks, that’s too good to be true
choices.feedback: Smart! Promises of huge, fast money are usually tricks.

choices.text: Yes! Here’s my $20, I can’t wait for $100!
choices.feedback: Careful! If it sounds too good to be true, it probably is.

end.speaker: Narwhal
end.text: Save some, know your profit, and watch out for tricks. You're a smart business owner!

a.speaker: Narwhal
a.text: You got your first paycheck from the bakery: $80! Your favorite shoes are $75. What's your plan?

choices.text: Save some, buy the shoes in a few weeks
choices.feedback: Planning big wants is smart.

choices.text: Buy the shoes right now and spend the rest too
choices.feedback: Okay, but now there's only $5 left for anything else.

b.speaker: Narwhal
b.text: Your little brother's birthday is next week. You'd like to get him a gift.

choices.text: Plan $10 for a gift from my paycheck
choices.feedback: Sharing is part of a good budget!

choices.text: Borrow money for a gift
choices.feedback: Borrowing for gifts can get tricky. Planning ahead works better.

c.speaker: Narwhal
c.text: Your boss offers more hours next month. That means less free time but more money. What do you think?

choices.text: Take a few extra hours and save for my goal
choices.feedback: Balancing time and money is a real trade-off. Nice!

choices.text: Work every free minute, even on school nights
choices.feedback: Money matters, but so do rest and friends. Balance is key!

end.speaker: Narwhal
end.text: You planned for wants, shared with family, and thought about time vs. money. That's real money wisdom!

a.speaker: Mayor Penny
a.text: The town wants a new playground. Where should the money come from?

choices.text: Everyone chips in a little through taxes
choices.feedback: Yes! Taxes let a whole town build things together.

choices.text: One kid pays for all of it
choices.feedback: That would be unfair and way too expensive for one person.

b.speaker: Mayor Penny
b.text: Which of these is paid for with taxes?

choices.text: Firefighters
choices.feedback: Right! Firefighters keep everyone safe.

choices.text: My new video game
choices.feedback: Families buy their own games. Taxes pay for things everyone shares.

c.speaker: Mayor Penny
c.text: Your paycheck says 'Earned $100, Take home $90.' Where did $10 go?

choices.text: Taxes for roads, schools and parks
choices.feedback: Exactly! That's why take-home pay is smaller.

choices.text: It disappeared because of a bank mistake
choices.feedback: It went to taxes, which pay for things we all use.

end.speaker: Narwhal
end.text: Taxes are how a community buys things together. Now you know where the money goes!

a.speaker: Max
a.text: I forgot my markers and we have art today. Can I borrow yours? I'll give them back after class.

choices.text: Sure, just give them back after class.
choices.feedback: Lending with a clear promise is kind and fair.

choices.text: No way, I don't lend my things to anybody, ever.
choices.feedback: It's okay to be careful, but Max hasn't broken a promise yet.

b.speaker: Narwhal
b.text: After class, Max gives every marker back, caps on. A week later Max asks again. What do you think?

choices.text: Yes! Max kept the promise last time.
choices.feedback: Right. Keeping promises builds trust, and trust is what lenders look for.

choices.text: No, I'm never lending anything to anyone again.
choices.feedback: Max proved they're trustworthy. Trust grows when promises are kept.

c.speaker: Narwhal
c.text: Another kid borrowed your markers and lost two. Who would you lend to next time?

choices.text: The friend who gave everything back
choices.feedback: Yes! Banks decide the same way. Paying back on time is called good credit.

choices.text: The friend who lost two, so they can make it up to me
choices.feedback: Lending again to someone who didn't keep their promise is risky.

end.speaker: Narwhal
end.text: Borrowing is a promise. Keep it, and people trust you more next time. Banks call that trust credit.

a.speaker: Max
a.text: I left my lunch money at home! Can I borrow $2? I'll pay you back Friday.

choices.text: Okay, $2 until Friday.
choices.feedback: A small loan with a clear date is a fair deal.

choices.text: Only if you pay me $10 back.
choices.feedback: That's way too much extra! Fair deals keep friends.

b.speaker: Max
b.text: It's Friday! Here's your $2, and an extra dime to say thanks.

choices.text: Thanks! You paid back on time.
choices.feedback: That extra dime is like interest: a small thank-you for lending.

choices.text: A dime? That's not nearly enough extra for waiting all week!
choices.feedback: It was a gift. The important part is Max paid back on time.

c.speaker: Narwhal
c.text: When grown-ups borrow from a bank, they pay back a little extra, called interest. Who pays LESS extra?

choices.text: People who always pay back on time
choices.feedback: Yes! Banks charge less to people they trust.

choices.text: People who forget to pay, since the bank feels sorry for them
choices.feedback: Banks charge more, or say no, when people don't pay back.

end.speaker: Narwhal
end.text: Borrow only what you can pay back, and pay on time. That's how trust, and good credit, are built.

a.speaker: Narwhal
a.text: The library lets you borrow three books for free for two weeks. What's the deal?

choices.text: I promise to bring them back on time
choices.feedback: Exactly. Borrowing always comes with a promise.

choices.text: I get to keep them forever since the library has so many books
choices.feedback: Borrowed things go back. That's what makes it borrowing.

b.speaker: Narwhal
b.text: Oops! One book is three days late. The library charges a late fee of 30 cents. Why?

choices.text: Because I broke the promise to return it on time
choices.feedback: Right. Late payments on loans cost extra too, called late fees.

choices.text: Because libraries are mean and just want to take kids' pocket money
choices.feedback: The fee reminds everyone to keep their promise so others can borrow.

c.speaker: Narwhal
c.text: Your friend always returns books on time. Their sister is always late. Who should the library trust with a special rare book?

choices.text: The friend who's always on time
choices.feedback: Yes! A history of keeping promises is what lenders trust.

choices.text: The sister who's always late, to give her one more chance to change
choices.feedback: Being late again and again makes it harder to be trusted.

end.speaker: Narwhal
end.text: Return things on time and pay back on time. People trust you more, and that trust is called credit.

a.speaker: Narwhal
a.text: You sold cookies at the school fair and made $26! The ingredients cost $8. How much profit did you make?

choices.feedback: Yes! Profit is what's left after costs: $26 minus $8.
That's all the money that came in. Take away the $8 of ingredients first.

b.speaker: Narwhal
b.text: Next fair, should you charge $1 or $5 for a cookie?

choices.text: $1, so lots of kids can buy one
choices.feedback: A fair price sells more. If it's too high, nobody buys.

choices.text: $5, so I make a lot more money on every single cookie
choices.feedback: You'd make more per cookie, but most kids would walk away.

c.speaker: Narwhal
c.text: You have $18 of profit. What's a smart plan?

choices.text: Save some, spend some, share some
choices.feedback: A great habit! Every jar gets a little.

choices.text: Spend it all today on something fun, I earned it after all
choices.feedback: Fun today, but nothing left for next fair's ingredients.

end.speaker: Narwhal
end.text: Know your costs, pick a fair price and save some profit. That's how a business keeps going!

a.speaker: Narwhal
a.text: You and your friend washed cars and made $44! Soap and sponges cost $8. What's the profit?

choices.feedback: Correct! $44 minus $8 of supplies.
Costs are taken away, not added. $44 minus $8.

b.speaker: Max
b.text: We both worked the whole time. How should we split the $36?

choices.text: $18 each, we worked the same
choices.feedback: Fair! Equal work, equal share.

choices.text: I keep $30 because it was my idea
choices.feedback: Ideas matter, but you both did the work. Fair splits keep partners happy.

c.speaker: Narwhal
c.text: Next Saturday it's raining and nobody comes. You still bought new soap. What happened?

choices.text: We had a cost but no sales, so we lost a little
choices.feedback: Yes. Businesses have bad days. Saving some profit helps cover them.

choices.text: Nothing happened, because rain doesn't change anything for a business
choices.feedback: No customers means no money in, but the soap still cost money.

end.speaker: Narwhal
end.text: Profit is money in minus costs. Split fairly, and save for rainy days, real or not!

a.speaker: Narwhal
a.text: Beads for one bracelet cost $1. You sell each bracelet for $3. How much do you make on each one?

choices.feedback: Right! $3 minus the $1 of beads.
Don't forget the beads cost $1 each.

b.speaker: Narwhal
b.text: A grown-up offers to buy all 10 bracelets for $5 total. Is that a good deal?

choices.text: No, that's only 50 cents each, less than the beads cost
choices.feedback: Yes! You'd lose money on every bracelet.

choices.text: Yes, selling all ten bracelets at once to one buyer is a great day for my business
choices.feedback: Selling everything sounds great, but $5 doesn't even cover $10 of beads.

c.speaker: Narwhal
c.text: Someone online says: send me $10 and I'll send you $100 of beads! What do you do?

choices.text: No thanks, it sounds too good to be true
choices.feedback: Smart! Deals that seem too good to be true usually are.

choices.text: Send the $10 right away before someone else grabs the deal
choices.feedback: That's a common trick. You'd likely lose your $10.

end.speaker: Narwhal
end.text: Know what each item costs you, never sell below cost, and watch out for tricks!

a.speaker: Narwhal
a.text: You worked 40 hours as a lifeguard at $10 an hour. Your paycheck says $400 earned, $352 take-home. Where did $48 go?

choices.text: Taxes, like Social Security and Medicare
choices.feedback: Right. Some pay goes to taxes before it reaches you.

choices.text: The pool kept it as a fee for giving me the lifeguard job
choices.feedback: Employers don't charge fees on pay. It's taxes withheld.

b.speaker: Narwhal
b.text: You want headphones that cost $150. What's your plan with the $352?

choices.text: Save part each payday and buy them in a few weeks
choices.feedback: Planning a want while still saving is a great habit.

choices.text: Buy them today and spend whatever is left on fun with friends
choices.feedback: You'd have the headphones, but no savings at all.

c.speaker: Max
c.text: Hey, you just got paid! Can I borrow $100? I'll pay you back... sometime.

choices.text: I can lend a little, but I need a clear payback date
choices.feedback: Kind and smart. A clear date protects the friendship.

choices.text: Sure, take the whole $100, whenever you get around to it is fine
choices.feedback: "Sometime" often means never. Agree on a date first.

end.speaker: Narwhal
end.text: Know where your pay goes, plan for wants and set clear terms when you lend.

a.speaker: Narwhal
a.text: You babysat on Saturday and earned $60 in cash. What should happen first?

choices.text: Put some in savings before spending
choices.feedback: Paying yourself first is a powerful habit.

choices.text: Keep it all in my pocket and spend it whenever something comes up
choices.feedback: Cash in a pocket tends to disappear. Give it a plan.

b.speaker: Narwhal
b.text: The family asks you to babysit every Saturday for $60. That's about $240 a month! What should you think about?

choices.text: Whether it fits with homework and other plans
choices.feedback: Yes. Time is valuable too. Money isn't the only thing to weigh.

choices.text: Nothing, more money is always better no matter how much time it takes
choices.feedback: More money is great, but not if your grades or sleep suffer.

c.speaker: Narwhal
c.text: A friend says cash from babysitting doesn't count as real income. Is that right?

choices.text: No, money you earn from work is income
choices.feedback: Correct. Cash or not, pay for work is income.

choices.text: Yes, cash is invisible, so it doesn't count as real money you earned
choices.feedback: Pay for work is income however it's paid.

end.speaker: Narwhal
end.text: Pay yourself first, weigh time against money and remember: what you earn is income.

a.speaker: Narwhal
a.text: Your café job pays by direct deposit. Where should the money go?

choices.text: Into a bank account I can see and track
choices.feedback: Direct deposit to a checking account is safe and easy to track.

choices.text: I'll ask to be paid in cash in an envelope
choices.feedback: Cash is harder to track and easy to lose.

b.speaker: Narwhal
b.text: You earned $300 plus $45 in tips this week. Your phone bill is $40. What's the plan?

choices.text: Pay the bill, save some, then plan fun money
choices.feedback: Bills first, then savings, then fun. Perfect order.

choices.text: Spend first, pay the bill if there's money left
choices.feedback: Bills can't wait. Late fees cost extra.

c.speaker: Narwhal
c.text: You see sneakers on sale for $120, today only! You had not planned to buy any. What do you do?

choices.text: Wait a day and decide if I really want them
choices.feedback: A 24-hour pause stops most impulse buys.

choices.text: Buy them now, because a sale this good might never come back again
choices.feedback: A sale on something you didn't plan to buy is still spending.

end.speaker: Narwhal
end.text: Track your pay, pay bills first, save next and pause before impulse buys.

a.speaker: Mayor Penny
a.text: The old bridge into town is cracked and must be fixed. It costs a lot. How should the town pay?

choices.text: Everyone chips in a little through taxes
choices.feedback: Yes. Taxes let a whole town pay for big things together.

choices.text: Whoever crosses first pays for all of it
choices.feedback: That's not fair. Everyone uses the bridge, so everyone shares the cost.

b.speaker: Mayor Penny
b.text: You buy shoes for $50, and the store adds $3 at the register. What is that $3?

choices.text: Sales tax
choices.feedback: Correct. Sales tax is added when you buy things.

choices.text: A tip for the cashier
choices.feedback: Tips are for service. The $3 is sales tax, which goes to the government.

c.speaker: Mayor Penny
c.text: The town has money for only one project this year: the bridge or a new fountain. Which first?

choices.text: The bridge, because people need it to get around safely
choices.feedback: Needs come before wants, for towns too.

choices.text: The fountain, because it's prettier and everyone will love taking photos
choices.feedback: Pretty, but the broken bridge is a safety problem.

end.speaker: Narwhal
end.text: Taxes pay for things a town needs together, and leaders choose needs first.

a.speaker: Mayor Penny
a.text: The library lends books to anyone for free. Who pays for the books and the librarians?

choices.text: Everyone, through taxes
choices.feedback: Right. Taxes keep the library free for everyone.

choices.text: The library prints its own money
choices.feedback: Only the government makes money, and it doesn't print it for libraries!

b.speaker: Mayor Penny
b.text: Which of these is NOT usually paid for with taxes?

choices.text: A family's pizza dinner
choices.feedback: Right. Families pay for their own food.

choices.text: Street lights that light up the sidewalks at night
choices.feedback: Street lights are public and paid for with taxes.

c.speaker: Mayor Penny
c.text: Your aunt's pay stub says Earned $500, Take home $440. Where did $60 go?

choices.text: Taxes, for schools, roads and parks
choices.feedback: Yes. Some pay goes to taxes before it reaches you.

choices.text: Her boss kept it for the office snack fund and birthday parties
choices.feedback: Bosses don't take pay for snacks. It's taxes.

end.speaker: Narwhal
end.text: Taxes are how a community shares the cost of things everyone uses.

a.speaker: Mayor Penny
a.text: A big snowstorm hit! Plows are clearing the roads. Who pays the plow drivers?

choices.text: The town, using taxes
choices.feedback: Right. Taxes pay for services everyone needs.

choices.text: Each driver pays for their own street
choices.feedback: That would leave many streets snowy. Sharing the cost works better.

b.speaker: Mayor Penny
b.text: What would happen if nobody paid any taxes?

choices.text: No plows, firefighters or public schools
choices.feedback: Exactly. Taxes keep those services running.

choices.text: Everything would stay the same, since services run on their own
choices.feedback: Public services need money to run.

c.speaker: Mayor Penny
c.text: A family earns more money than another. In many places, they pay a higher share in income tax. What's the idea?

choices.text: People who earn more can chip in more
choices.feedback: That's called a progressive tax.

choices.text: It's a punishment for working hard and earning a lot of money
choices.feedback: It's not a punishment. It's a way of sharing costs by ability to pay.

end.speaker: Narwhal
end.text: Taxes keep roads clear, schools open and helpers on the job. Everyone shares the cost.
